definition: In this historical source, a tautology is a statement that is true only because it restates the same relation in different words, without adding any concrete information. It is used to criticize formulas like “identity in difference” when they do not specify what the actual likenesses or differences are.

provenance.revision: 1901 New York Macmillan original; archive index checked 2026-10-18
provenance.scope: Source record Identitym; pinned source text

reasons: The packet does not define “tautology” as a statement “true only because it restates the same relation in different words.” It only says that a certain criticism is “mere tautology” in relation to concrete matters of fact.

The packet does not explicitly describe tautology as lacking added “concrete information”; it discusses that determining “identity in difference” “says nothing as to the extent or form” of likenesses/differences, but this is not stated as a general definition of tautology.

The example references “identity in difference” and discusses what it does not determine, but the definition’s formulation (“restates the same relation…”) is not directly supported by the supplied text.
